title: Debt Collection Timelines After a Death: November 2026 Guide
summary: See how long creditors have to collect debt after a death in 2026, plus how probate deadlines limit claims against the estate.
body_markdown:
After someone dies, creditors may try to collect money the person owed at the time of death. These debts are generally paid from the estate, not by relatives. Whether a creditor can still collect depends on state law and two separate deadlines: the time to sue over the debt and the time to file a claim against the estate. This guide explains key points for families and executors to be aware of, including: who is responsible for debt after death, how long creditors have to sue, probate claim deadlines, rules in selected states, which debts get paid first, and more.


**Key Takeaways**


- Debt lawsuit deadlines and probate claim deadlines both affect collection after death.
- Many states allow 3 to 6 years to sue over debt.
- Estates generally pay debts. Relatives owe only if they share legal liability or an exception applies.
- Elayne organizes estate assets and debts into an inventory with sources for review before payment.


## What Happens to Debt When Someone Dies?


Debt generally remains owed after someone dies. The estate is the money and property the person left behind. The Consumer Financial Protection Bureau explains that[debts are generally paid](https://www.consumerfinance.gov/ask-cfpb/does-a-persons-debt-go-away-when-they-die-en-1463/) from the estate.


Valid debts are paid from available estate assets before heirs receive their inheritance, subject to state-law protections and exceptions.

## Does Debt Transfer to Family Members?


Relatives generally do not inherit debt when someone dies. The CFPB's family debt responsibility rules explain exceptions:


- Co-signers can remain responsible for loans they signed.
- Joint credit card account holders can owe the balance; authorized users generally do not share that liability.
- Surviving spouses may owe certain debts under state law, depending on the debt involved.


A collector's call alone does not make a family member responsible for payment.


## Probate Claim Deadlines and Debt Statutes of Limitations


The statute of limitations on debt after death and the probate claim deadline limit different steps. Both can apply to the same debt.


Timeframe What it limits


Debt statute of limitations Time to sue over the debt


Probate claim deadline Time to submit a claim against the estate


## How the Probate Process Governs Creditor Claims


The executor or personal representative[notifies creditors and manages estate debt](https://www.elayne.com/resources/notify-creditors-manage-estate-debt-executors) under state probate rules. This can involve direct notice to known creditors and publication in a qualifying newspaper.


A published Notice to Creditors can start the period for creditors to submit claims for payment from the estate.


Creditors who miss the applicable deadline after proper notice may lose the right to collect from the estate. The consequences depend on state law, the notice provided, and any exceptions.


## Debt Statute of Limitations by State: How Long Creditors Have to Sue


In many states, creditors have[three to six years](https://www.consumerfinance.gov/ask-cfpb/can-debt-collectors-collect-a-debt-thats-several-years-old-en-1423/) to sue over debts, according to the CFPB, though some states allow longer. The statute of limitations on debt can differ for written contracts, credit cards, and oral agreements.


The credit agreement may name another state's law as governing, even if the person who died lived elsewhere. For executors reviewing old balances, the agreement and debt type help identify the applicable deadline; the person's last residence alone may not determine it.


## State-Specific Rules: California, New York, New Jersey, Pennsylvania, and Georgia


Debt and probate deadlines differ; exceptions apply to these selected rules.


State Time to sue Probate rule


California Written:[4 years](https://law.justia.com/codes/california/code-ccp/part-2/title-2/chapter-3/section-337/) Separate one-year-after-death limit often applies


New York Consumer:[3 years](https://www.nysenate.gov/legislation/laws/CVP/214-I) Distribution protection after[7 months](https://www.nysenate.gov/legislation/laws/SCP/1802) from appointment

Pennsylvania Contracts: generally 4 years Distribution protection:[one year after advertisement](https://www.palegis.us/statutes/consolidated/view-statute?txtType=HTM&ttl=20&div=00.&chpt=035.&sctn=032.&subsctn=000.)

Distribution protections do not erase debts.


## Which Debts Get Paid First: Priority of Claims in an Estate


State law sets estate payment priorities; filing first does not guarantee payment first. Common claim categories include:


- Estate administration expenses and funeral costs.
- Secured debts, with rights tied to collateral.
- Federal and state taxes.
- Unsecured debts, including credit cards and[medical bills after death](https://www.elayne.com/resources/medical-bills-hospital-debt-after-death-legal-responsibility) .


This list is not a universal payment order. Rankings vary by state, and collateral rights and federal tax priority can affect payment. An estate is insolvent when assets cannot cover debts and expenses; lower-priority creditors may receive little or nothing.


## Rules Debt Collectors Must Follow When Someone Has Died


Under federal debt collection protections, collectors may discuss debts with executors or administrators. They cannot falsely claim that relatives are personally responsible for payment. Contact with other relatives is generally limited to[locating the estate representative](https://www.consumerfinance.gov/ask-cfpb/can-a-debt-collector-contact-me-about-a-deceased-relatives-debts-en-1469/) , without discussing the debt.

## How Elayne Helps Executors Manage Estate Debts


[Elayne](https://www.elayne.com/company) is an online service that helps families settle an estate after a death, one step at a time. For estate debts, Elayne gathers records of what the person owed, organizes them in one place, and flags open items for review. The executor or personal representative holds the legal authority (letters testamentary or letters of administration) to act for the estate, including paying valid claims under state law. The family's attorney advises on areas such as creditor claims and deadlines and works from the same estate record.


### **Finding what the person owed**


Elayne Asset Search (IRS authorization · Equifax) looks for debts alongside assets. It requests the person's Equifax credit report, which lists open accounts, credit cards, loans, and credit lines in their name.


Elayne also holds IRS authorization to request 10 years of the person's IRS tax transcripts. An IRS tax transcript is not a tax return. It is a record of what banks, lenders, employers, and insurers reported about the person to the IRS, so the IRS tax transcripts can point to accounts and lenders that had a financial relationship with the person.


The IRS tax transcripts also show whether the estate owes the IRS anything, such as a balance due or unfiled years.


### **An estate inventory with sources**


Each debt Elayne locates is added to the estate inventory, similar to[listing assets and debts for probate](https://www.elayne.com/resources/how-to-list-assets-and-debts-for-the-court-during-probate) . Every entry names the institution that reported it and the record it came from. Debts appear in the same inventory as retirement accounts, bank accounts, life insurance, and property, so the estate's obligations are visible before anything is paid out.


A debt in the inventory is a reported debt. Whether the estate pays it depends on state law, the debt statute of limitations, and the probate claim deadline, which the attorney reviews.


### **Protecting the person's credit and mail**


Through Estate Setup, Elayne sends the deceased notification to the credit bureaus, so no new credit can be opened in the person's name. Elayne also places a "Do not mail" hold, and mail forwarding is listed as a time-sensitive step so tax forms and legal mail reach the family.


### **Recording payments and the final accounting**


With Elayne's Estate Settlement option, the estate bank account is connected to Elayne. Each deposit and payment is recorded, with a note each time money moves, and the attorney can see this activity without needing a bank login. Costs the executor paid personally are tracked with receipts and paid back as money comes in.


Elayne hands over the final accounting: every payment and deposit, with receipts attached, ready for the court, the attorney, and the people receiving what remains. Decisions about which debts are paid, and in what order, stay with the executor, with the attorney advising. Elayne is an eligible estate expense, paid from the estate account or reimbursed by it. Court, attorney, and other professional fees are separate.


## FAQ


### Does an old debt have to be paid just because it appears in an Elayne estate inventory?


No. An inventory entry documents a reported debt; it does not prove that the estate must pay it. Before payment, an attorney can review the statute of limitations on debt, the probate claim deadline, and whether a payment could restart the lawsuit clock under applicable state law.


### Can an executor rely on Elayne alone if a collector sues over a deceased person's debt after 7 years?


No. Elayne organizes estate records, while an attorney advises on responding to a lawsuit and any deadline defenses. Seven years is not a universal cutoff for suing over debt, and a court response may still be required even when the debt is past the statute of limitations.


### How are records organized in Elayne for an attorney reviewing creditor deadlines?


The review starts with the credit agreement, payment history, collection letters, creditor notices, and any probate claim filings. Keeping these documents in Elayne's shared estate record gives an attorney the dates and supporting records needed to review both the lawsuit deadline and the probate claim deadline.


### Who has legal authority to pay a deceased person's debts?


The executor or personal representative appointed by the court holds that authority. When there is a will, the court issues letters testamentary to the named executor. When there is no will, the court appoints an administrator, who receives letters of administration.


Some states use a small estate affidavit to give a named person limited authority without a full appointment. Relatives without court authority generally cannot pay debts from estate assets.
